Now is officially the worst time to buy a NAS—here's what I'm doing instead

Link copied to clipboard
By  Patrick Campanale
Published Mar 20, 2026, 10:00 AM EDT

Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents:
Try something different:

Having a NAS in a homelab is crucial, but 2026 is probably the worst time I’ve ever seen to buy a brand-new NAS. So, instead, I turn to the one place that hasn’t been revenged by supply shortages—the used market.

✕ Remove Ads

I’m tired of underpowered NAS CPUs

And powerful models are absurdly expensive

When looking for a new NAS, it’s going to be hard to find one that comes with an Intel x86 processor at a reasonable price. There are systems like the TERRAMASTER F2-425, but outside of that one, typically most NAS servers under $500 have Arm processors in them.

✕ Remove Ads

Don’t get me wrong, Arm can be extremely powerful when done right. But, the Rockchip processors that are in most NAS units just aren’t all that powerful. Those chips can handle transcoding decently, but nothing like what a proper x86 Intel CPU can.

Stepping into systems that have proper Core i5 or Core Ultra i5 processors can easily put you into the $800 to $1,000 or more range for a NAS, which is absurd.

✕ Remove Ads

Right now is one of the worst time to buy a NAS because computer components are just insanely overpriced due to memory shortages making RAM more difficult to obtain. So, instead of buying a new NAS, going with an old, repurposed computer is a far better option.

Old office PCs make great NAS alternatives

They’re cheaper and far more capable

When building a new NAS, the first place I go is Facebook Marketplace to look for old, retired office PCs. You’d be surprised at the deals that you can find on Marketplace for a used PC.

✕ Remove Ads

For example, in the pictures above, there are multiple desktops that can be purchased second-hand with specs that would destroy any $400-$500 NAS. In fact, most of the desktops would even outperform a $1,000 NAS for many tasks.

Not only does an old office or gaming PC have solid power, but they’re often far more flexible and capable than a cheaper NAS. The TERRAMASTER NAS I mentioned above can only hold two hard drives and doesn’t have any capability for SSD caching. Each desktop in the screenshots above can handle more than two hard drives and also offers SSD caching, either through a SATA drive or some even have NVMe capabilities.

✕ Remove Ads

I always start with an older office PC from Marketplace when building a more budget-friendly NAS because it’s simply more economical. It keeps the desktop from going to the landfill, and gives me a more upgradable NAS for less money.

Even older Intel CPUs can outperform many NAS processors

Especially for running Plex on a NAS

✕ Remove Ads

Each desktop in the screenshots above features an Intel processor that has QuickSync capabilities—or the desktop already comes with an NVIDIA GPU pre-installed. Having Intel QuickSync or an NVIDIA GPU is crucial for transcoding on Plex (or even Jellyfin).

NVIDIA and Intel simply have transcoding dialed in and perform the best regardless of what software you use. So, that’s another reason I love choosing a used PC over a pre-built NAS. I already mentioned it’s hard to find an Intel-based NAS for cheap, and transcoding is the primary reason that I always go Intel for my NAS servers whenever I can.

✕ Remove Ads

Choosing what OS the NAS runs is half the fun

I almost always pick Unraid, but there are many other options

Many NAS operating systems are locked down from accessing features that users could otherwise benefit from. I have a 2016-model Synology NAS at my church, and I can’t run Docker on it because Synology hasn’t (and won’t) enable it for hardware that old. The hardware is capable of it, though things would run slow. But, since it doesn’t give the “desired” feel, Synology won’t enable it.

✕ Remove Ads

That’s why I really do prefer to build my own custom NAS systems since I get to choose the operating system, which, in turn, lets me pick the feature set.

For example, I recently deployed the Ugreen iDX6011 Pro NAS in my homelab—it’s a beats. However, I can’t mix-and-match hard drive sizes in it like I typically prefer to do because UGOS Pro only supports normal RAID types. My favorite NAS OS, Unraid, lets you mix multiple drive sizes together into one large pool—similar to TRAID on TERRAMASTER or SHR on Synology.

✕ Remove Ads

That’s just one example of why picking my own operating system for my own NAS is the way I prefer to go. Another is that the community often supports hardware for far longer than a manufacturer does. My main storage server is from 2014, and my other two rack-mount servers I had were from 2012.

Even though those older servers are old by technology standards, and are no longer officially supported by their manufacturer, I was easily able to install a modern OS on them and get modern features, like Docker, virtual machine support, and more. Those types of functions just aren’t available on older NAS units, making retired desktops that much better for using as a NAS in my workflow.

Building a NAS is just the best option right now

While buying a pre-built NAS is a little more convenient, as it’s ready to go out of the box, building one is just the best option in the current computer climate. It’s far easier to get more power for less money when buying a used desktop instead of a pre-built NAS, which is why that’s what I’ll continue to do for the foreseeable future.
